reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

THE MOUNT AND THE UNMOUNT AS ONE OPERATION, because half of a subscription is not a thing a screen ever does. The only subscriber is an effect. Ours allocates a `TOIMEffect`, files it on the slot's effect list and holds the slot, asks whether the slot was written since the batch opened so a write already in it still reaches the newcomer, and on the way out clears its pending mark, swaps itself out of the list, unholds the slot and asks whether anything still keeps it. The one-element source array is built outside the clock, per slot, so the caller's literal is not charged. The floor adds to a `Set` somebody else has to remember to create, and can never tell the new subscriber about a write that already landed. Direction: inflates our ratio. Every slot here carries a value, so the unhold never releases an identity.

reading.floor: const held = byId.get(row.id); if (held === undefined) byId.set(row.id, { ...row })
reading.caveat: THE ANCHOR ROW, AND THE ONLY ONE HERE WHOSE RATIO MEANS ANYTHING: the floor is `baseline-array.ts`'s insert copied, so this is the engine half of the scenario gap. IT IS NOT THE WHOLE SCENARIO GAP AND MUST NOT BE READ AS ONE. The `oimdb` adapter keeps its group index inside its own `write`, and `baseline-array` deliberately keeps no index at all. None of that bookkeeping is on either side of this pair. In our favour: our side takes no frame and flushes nothing, so no delivery is timed on either side. Against us: our side mints a fourteen-field slot, opens and closes a change window, stamps the clock and marks the slot on the channel per row, which the floor has no equivalent of.

reading.ours: collection.fillContents(keys, rows) — mint and set, no probe
reading.floor: collection.upsertEntities(rows) — probe, then mint and set
reading.caveat: BOTH ARMS ARE OURS AND THE FIGURE IS THE DIFFERENCE, NOT THE RATIO. `fillContents` files every key without asking whether it is taken, on a precondition — this collection holds nothing — checked once per call rather than per row; `upsertEntities` asks per row through `writeByKey`. So the difference is one string hash on a `Map` that grows to the population size, plus `fillContents`'s own duplicate check — which is a second `get` per row on `fillContents`'s side, so the two arms hash equally often and THIS ROW NOW PRICES THE WRITE DOOR'S FRAMING, NOT A HASH: `writeByKey`'s per-row change window and `keyOf` call against `fillContents`'s one window per call. reading.ours: updateEntity(slot, { group }) with an OIMIndex over group, then index.getBucketMemberSlots(bucket) — the auto-index, in place
reading.floor: move the row between two Sets, write the column, iterate one Set
reading.caveat: THE ARM IS THE AUTO-INDEX, IN PLACE. THE MOVE IS THE ENGINE'S: the index listens to the collection's content changes, so `updateEntity` alone re-files the row — `updateIndexKeyForSlot` reads the previous key off the slot's index-key cell, runs `keyOf` on the new entity, writes the cell, and calls `removeBucketMemberSlotByKey` and `addBucketMemberSlotByKey`, each a hash of the address, a `Set` edit, a hold or an unhold and a channel mark queued to the change close. A caller writes one call and cannot forget to move a row. [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE] Expect this to be the closest arm of the task; if a manual door comes out closer, the listener path costs more than the caller writing the move. THE FLOOR IS THE SAME CODE FOR EVERY ARM OF THIS TASK, which is the property that makes the arms comparable at all. It moves the row between two `Set`s — the container our unordered bucket holds its members in, so this is the structural equal and not a cheaper shape — writes the column, and iterates one group. WHAT IT DOES LESS OF, and every item pushes our ratio UP: it keeps no identity that outlives the value, so nothing can be subscribed to a row or to a group; it stamps no clock; it records no moved columns; it keeps no hold count, so a group cannot be resolved by address and handed to a consumer; and its groups can be read by iterating them and by nothing else. WHAT IS ON BOTH SIDES AND CANCELS: the read group is held from outside the clock on both, and the read visits the same members on both. WHERE THE FLOOR IS CHARGED MORE THAN IT SHOULD BE, stated because it flatters us: it hashes `row.group` to find the departure set, where the index arm reads the previous key off the slot's own index-key cell.

reading.ours: updateEntity(slot, { group }), writeContent on both buckets, then getBucketMemberSlots(bucket)
reading.floor: move the row between two Sets, write the column, iterate one Set
reading.caveat: THE ARM IS THE WHOLE-BUCKET DOOR, IN PLACE. THE MEMBERSHIP IS THE CALLER'S ON THIS ARM: the bucket collection is not an index and hears no write, so the move is made in the same statement sequence as the write, inside the timed body. WHAT THE ARM PAYS THAT THE FLOOR DOES NOT: `updateEntity` walks the patch, gates the column, builds the moved-column list and marks the row on the channel; then the move marks both buckets and keeps the slot's hold count. THE ADDRESS IS RESOLVED THE SAME WAY ON BOTH SIDES: one `getSlotByKey` per end of the move, which is the hash the floor pays as `byGroup.get(next)`. THE OLD GROUP IS READ OFF THE STORED ROW BEFORE THE WRITE LANDS, which a caller holding the slot can always do. `writeContent` is handed each bucket's new membership, asks the bucket service whether the bucket already holds exactly those slots, and — since it does not — replaces the set and reports who arrived and who left. Moving one row is therefore TWO FULL BUCKET REWRITES, plus the caller's own `indexOf` and `splice` on the array it keeps beside them, on groups of a hundred and twenty-eight. THIS IS THE DOOR A RE-HYDRATED SERVER LIST USES and pricing it on a one-row move is pricing it on its worst task; the distance between it and the other arms is what the finer doors are worth. reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) with the values the row already holds — the shipped default, no index
reading.floor: map.get(id), then compare each column and assign only what moved
reading.caveat: THE ARM IS THE SHIPPED DEFAULT, NO INDEX. NOTHING MOVES ON EITHER SIDE, which is the point of the task: `upsertEntity` finds the key populated, `OIMEntityCollection.writeEntity` walks the stored row for columns the new one does not carry (there are none), calls `patchEntity`, is told nothing moved, and `write` returns before it marks anything or tells any listener. The floor gets the row and compares. THIS IS THE FAIREST FLOOR IN THE SUITE: a hand-written store that wanted to wake anybody would need the same decision this write makes. WHERE THE FLOOR STILL DOES LESS, both pushing our ratio UP: it compares four columns named at compile time where `patchEntity` enumerates whatever the patch carries, and it never looks for columns the stored row has that the new one does not, where `writeEntity` walks the stored row with a `hasOwnProperty` per column first. Ours also opens and closes a change window per row. THE HASH IS ON BOTH SIDES: ours calls `keyOf` and the store's `get`, the floor calls `byId.get`. THE FLUSH IS INSIDE OUR NUMBER and closes a batch that queued nothing. NO INDEX IS BUILT on this arm, which is the baseline the indexed arm is read against. THE SAME SOURCE ROWS ARE RE-SENT EVERY PASS, so no pass can drift into being a real write.

reading.ours: updateEntity(slot, { rank }), then sortedComputedCollection.getValueForSlot(sortedComputed) —createOIMComputedCollectionSorted over an index, columns [rank asc]
reading.floor: swap the ranks, then indexOf/splice out and upperBound/splice in, on a sorted array
reading.caveat: AN ENTITY MOVES WITHIN ITS GROUP, NOTHING JOINS OR LEAVES. A frame swaps the ranks of band `m` and band `m + 64` in every one of the sixty-four groups for 4 values of `m`, so each group of 128 sees 8 movers. OURS IS THE SHIPPED ORDER: an `OIMIndex` over `group` (`createOIMIndexSetDriven`) and a `createOIMComputedCollectionSorted` over it with `columns: [{ column: 'rank', direction: 'asc' }]`, one sorted computed held per group. NOTHING IS REPORTED BY HAND: `updateEntity` hands the index the changed columns, the index writes the group's `rank` bucket column slot, and that slot is a source of the group's sorted computed. THE READ IS INSIDE THE TIMED BODY: the computed is pulled, so the sort runs at the first `getValueForSlot` of the frame and every group is walked once per frame on both sides. THE COUNT THIS PREDICTS, per group per frame: ours copies the previous order (`slice` of 128) and runs `Array.prototype.sort` over it with the columns comparator, each compare loading `entity` off two slots and reading `rank` off both; the floor does, per mover, `indexOf`, `splice` out, `upperBoundByRank` and `splice` in. [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE] V8's sort over 128 entries with 8 displaced is on the order of 128 compares plus a binary search per mover, against the floor's 8 scans and 16 splices. WHERE THEY ARE NOT EQUAL: ours re-sorts the whole group however few entities moved, where the floor touches only the movers, which inflates our ratio; ours sorts once for all eight movers, which flatters us; and ours additionally walks the patch, marks the entity slot and the bucket column slot on the channel per `updateEntity`, which the floor's plain field store does not.

reading.ours: buckets.getSlotByKey([deckSlot, shelfSlot]) on a tree-driven bucket store
reading.caveat: AN ADDRESS OF TWO IDENTITIES AGAINST AN ADDRESS OF TWO STRINGS. Ours walks the composite key tree `OIMSlotStoreServiceTreeDriven` keeps: one `Map.get` keyed by the deck slot, one keyed by the shelf slot, then the bucket on the node — object-keyed hashes, no string hashing. The floor makes two string-keyed `Map.get`s and an `undefined` test. The key arrays are built outside the clock, as a caller holding the two segment identities would hold the pair. Every address hits a held bucket, so `getSlotByKey` never mints; it adds the store call and the `found !== undefined` test over the floor. Sixty-four combinations, eight decks by eight shelves, cycled on both sides. It replaces `chain-address.resolve-and-hold-vs-nested-map-get`, which held per call; no reading was ever recorded under either id.
